periods.analysis: Restaurant inspection compliance was 93.6%, above the >=92% target and in green status for the opening quarter of this review. With no prior-quarter value in this series, I read this as a solid baseline rather than a victory lap: most establishments are controlling the routine risks that make people sick, especially cold holding, handwashing, and sanitizer concentration. The Environmental Health team completed the summer route cycle in the Waterfront, Eastgate, and Old Harbor dining corridors, with extra attention to high-volume patio kitchens during tourism season. From a population-health standpoint, this means we are preventing foodborne illness before it reaches clinics, schools, or emergency departments.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by keeping the risk-based inspection calendar intact and protecting inspector time on the Friday-Monday peak-service route blocks. Extend the prevention work by offering two short ServSafe refresher clinics in English and Spanish for establishments with new managers or repeated temperature-control findings. Use the Q3 baseline to flag any facility with two consecutive minor violations for a coaching visit before it becomes an enforcement case.

periods.analysis: Compliance rose to 93.8%, a quarter-over-quarter increase of 0.2 percentage points from 93.6%, and remained green against the >=92% target. The movement is small but useful because Q4 includes holiday catering, temporary event kitchens, and staff turnover in quick-service restaurants. Inspectors used the Harborview Holiday Food Safety Sweep to cover caterers near Pier 6, banquet halls on Alder Avenue, and pop-up vendors tied to the winter market. The result suggests the prevention message held during a higher-volume, higher-risk period.
periods.recommendations: Maintain the Holiday Food Safety Sweep next year, but start the caterer outreach two weeks earlier so corrective actions are complete before peak bookings. Continue same-week rechecks for critical violations, especially hot holding and cross-contamination, because that is where illness risk changes fastest. Add a simple post-inspection handout for seasonal food workers so the compliance gain is not dependent only on managers.

periods.analysis: Compliance was 93.6%, down 0.2 percentage points from 93.8%, but still green and safely above the >=92% target. The slight decline is not clinically alarming, though it is a reminder that winter staffing churn and new ownership transfers can erode basic controls. The team saw several first-quarter onboarding issues along the Route 14 and North Marina corridors, mostly incomplete illness policies and inconsistent sanitizer logs rather than broad kitchen failure. The quarter continues the pattern of strong population-level protection with a small watch item around newly permitted operators.
periods.recommendations: Sustain green performance by keeping new-owner inspections within the first 45 days of permit transfer. Extend the onboarding packet into a brief required virtual orientation for new food-safety managers, with emphasis on employee illness exclusion and sanitizer verification. Ask inspectors to tag new establishments in the EnerGov record so we can compare their compliance trend separately next quarter.

periods.analysis: Compliance improved to 95.6%, up 2.0 percentage points from 93.6%, the strongest result so far and well above the >=92% target. This is the kind of improvement we want: not just more inspections, but earlier correction of predictable risks before the summer surge. The Spring Start Clean campaign paired routine inspections with coaching visits at school-adjacent cafés, food trucks staging at Bayfront Park, and seafood vendors reopening extended hours. The data indicate that targeted prevention, especially before peak service months, is translating into safer food environments across the city.
periods.recommendations: Continue Spring Start Clean as an annual pre-summer intervention and reserve two inspector days each April for food-truck commissary checks. Extend the coaching model to establishments with prior cooling or date-marking violations, because those risks are common and preventable. Preserve the current inspection cadence through summer by using part-time environmental health aides for data entry and permit file cleanup, not field judgment.

periods.analysis: Compliance was 94.5%, down 1.1 percentage points from 95.6%, but it remained green and comfortably above the >=92% target. The decline is expected after an unusually strong Q2 and during the busiest coastal dining quarter, when temporary events and high table turnover test kitchen routines. Inspectors reported heavier loads from the Harbor Lights Festival, Pier 3 seafood tents, and late-night vendors near the ferry terminal, with most corrections handled on site. The key point is that the system absorbed summer pressure without falling below the public-health standard.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the summer event inspection model, including pre-opening checks for festival vendors and on-site correction logs. For next Q3, extend the temporary food vendor briefing to include a five-minute cooling and reheating demonstration, not just paperwork review. Keep a watch list of repeat event vendors with prior critical violations and schedule them for the first inspection wave rather than waiting for complaint triggers.

periods.analysis: Compliance declined to 93.5%, down 1.0 percentage point from 94.5%, while staying green above the >=92% target. Two consecutive quarterly declines deserve attention even though the level remains strong; prevention work is most valuable before a green measure becomes a yellow one. The Q4 pattern was concentrated in establishments with new shift leads after autumn hiring, particularly along the Southpoint retail corridor and the Harborview Mall food court. We are still seeing manageable issues, but the margin over target narrowed compared with mid-2025.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the inspection schedule, but add a focused Q1 retraining push for establishments with management turnover documented in their permit file. Extend direct outreach to mall and corridor operators by offering a 30-minute group session on active managerial control before the lunch rush season. Review the top five violation categories from Q4 and assign each inspector one prevention script to use consistently during routine visits.

periods.analysis: Compliance rebounded to 95.3%, up 1.8 percentage points from 93.5%, returning the measure close to its 2025-Q2 high and clearly green. That rebound suggests the late-2025 watch item was real but responsive to intervention, not a structural weakening of the program. The January Manager Reset sessions at the Civic Health Annex, combined with targeted rechecks for Southpoint and mall operators, appear to have improved active managerial control. From a prevention lens, this is a good example of using inspection data to intervene early rather than waiting for outbreaks or complaints.
periods.recommendations: Keep the Manager Reset sessions as a standing first-quarter practice and invite every facility with a new certified food protection manager. Extend the targeted recheck protocol for facilities with repeated cold-holding or handwashing findings, with rechecks scheduled within 10 business days. Document which establishments attended training so we can compare their Q2 compliance against non-attendees and refine the program.

periods.analysis: Compliance reached 96.3%, up 1.0 percentage point from 95.3%, the highest value in the series and well above the >=92% target. The improvement continues the rebound that began in 2026-Q1 and shows that prevention activities are compounding rather than fading. Inspectors completed the Pre-Summer Safe Service route for Bayfront Park vendors, Old Harbor restaurants, and commissary kitchens serving mobile units, with fewer repeat critical violations than last year. The result is strong, but the public-health obligation remains the same: keep the controls reliable before high-volume summer service begins.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the Pre-Summer Safe Service route and lock it into the annual inspection calendar before special-event permits are finalized. Extend the approach by creating a small peer-mentor cohort of high-compliance operators to model temperature logs, illness policies, and corrective-action records for newer businesses. Continue monthly review of repeat critical violations so the 96.3% performance becomes a durable safety floor, not a one-quarter peak.

periods.analysis: The carried-forward June compliance rate of 96.3% exceeds the 92% target. It reflects the strong pre-summer inspection baseline, not a measured September improvement.
periods.recommendations: Reconcile September inspection and repeat-violation records before reporting a Q3 change, and maintain checks on high-volume and temporary-event food service.
